title: The Damascus road (Acts 9:1–19)
hook: Saul the persecutor is knocked down, blinded, and becomes Paul

segments.voice: Yesterday, Stephen, whom the Church calls the first martyr, praying for the people throwing the stones. Your line was lord, lay not this sin. And a young man named Saul stood holding their coats. Day seventy-six.

Saul is sure. That's the thing to understand about him. He's a devout, brilliant Pharisee, and he's certain these followers of Jesus are dangerous. After Stephen, he goes house to house in Jerusalem, dragging people off to prison. Then he asks the high priest for letters so he can do the same in Damascus, far to the north. He's on the road, nearly there, when a light from heaven flashes around him, and he falls to the ground. And a voice, in the Douay-Rheims: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" Today: a man stopped in his tracks, and a road with a name.
screen: `SAUL IS SURE.` → `LETTERS FOR DAMASCUS.` → `SAUL, SAUL, WHY PERSECUTEST THOU ME?`

segments.voice: Saul asks who's speaking. The answer: "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest." Notice: not my followers. Me. Catholics hear this as the heart of what the Church is, the body of Christ. Hurt his people and you hurt him. Saul gets up, opens his eyes, and can't see a thing. His companions lead him by the hand into Damascus, where he sits three days without eating or drinking. Meanwhile, the Lord speaks to a disciple in Damascus named Ananias and tells him: go to Saul. Ananias, very reasonably, objects. This man? The one who came here to arrest us? Go, he's told. He's my chosen instrument. So Ananias goes. And his first words to the man who came to put him in chains are: "Brother Saul." He lays his hands on him, and, in the Douay-Rheims: "immediately there fell from his eyes as it were scales, and he received his sight." That's where we get the phrase the scales fell from my eyes. Two things the story doesn't say. First, there's no horse. Saul falls to the ground, but the horse comes from later paintings. Second, God doesn't rename him on the road. A few chapters later Acts simply says Saul was also called Paul, and from then on Luke uses Paul. Some readers take them as his Jewish and Roman names. And the man who came to Damascus to put people in chains spends the rest of Acts carrying the name he tried to silence. Catholics keep the feast of his conversion on January twenty-fifth.
screen: `NOT MY FOLLOWERS. ME.` · `THREE DAYS BLIND.` · `ANANIAS: BROTHER SAUL.` · `NO HORSE, NO RENAMING.` · then, large: `THERE FELL FROM HIS EYES AS IT WERE SCALES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for your own blind spot. Settle and breathe. Saul wasn't a bad man trying to do wrong. He was sure he was right. So think of something you're very sure about, especially about a person or a group. Ask gently: is there anything I'm not seeing? Don't force an answer. Just leave the door open a crack. And think of Ananias too: is there someone you'd be afraid to call brother or sister? If you pray, you can ask to see. The bell holds the time.
The Damascus road. Where Saul, so sure he was right, was knocked down, blinded, and turned around. Today's word.
Your line: the scales fall. Today, change your mind about one small thing, out loud, when someone shows you you're wrong. Day seventy-six.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the Feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul on 25 January, and many use the phrase a Damascus road for any sudden turning of heart.

myth: Acts never mentions a horse. it comes from later paintings.
God changed Saul's name to Paul on the road
there's no renaming on the road. Acts later says Saul was also called Paul, and Luke starts using Paul.
he reminds the Lord that Saul came to arrest them. then he goes anyway.

fork.setup: you're Ananias. the Lord tells you to go to the man who came to Damascus to arrest you. what do you do?
fork.reveal: he objects honestly, then goes, and his first words are "brother Saul."

original.note: Greek: scales, flakes, like a fish's. what fell from Saul's eyes.

trapdoor: what you thought: Saul fell off his horse, saw a light, and got a new name.
what it means: a man sure he was right hears Jesus say, why do you persecute me, and is healed by one of the people he came to arrest.
what a scholar hears: no horse and no renaming in Acts. and 'me, not my followers' is where Catholics hear the Church as the body of Christ.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Acts 9:4, 9:5, 9:17 and 9:18 given from memory; confirm.
Distance Jerusalem–Damascus: roughly 135–150 miles depending on route; script says 'a hundred and fifty miles'. Confirm.
The horse is absent from Acts 9, 22 and 26; it enters through later art (e.g. Caravaggio). Confirm.
Saul/Paul: Acts 13:9 'Saul, who also is Paul'. Paul held Roman citizenship (Acts 22:28). Confirm phrasing.
'Wrote much of the New Testament': thirteen letters bear his name; scholars differ on how many he wrote himself. Keeper may want 'letters that fill much of the New Testament'.
Church as the body of Christ, linked to Acts 9:4–5 in Catholic teaching (CCC 787–795; Augustine). Confirm.
'Pharisee' from Philippians 3:5 and Acts 23:6; described respectfully.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the uncited 'hundred and fifty miles', 'the most famous turnaround in history' and 'the greatest missionary the Church ever had... wrote much of the New Testament' (superlatives and an authorship claim); Saul/Paul now follows Acts 13:9 ('also called Paul') with the Hebrew/Roman reading as 'some readers'; Acts 9:2 has Saul asking for the letters; review calls Stephen the first martyr as the Church's title; Ananias myth now says 'objected', not 'afraid'; added Acts 23:6 and the 25 January calendar source.
